title: Bowing lessons from Wallace, president of Local 47
summary: Wallace, a trombone and bass man who played with Whiteman, teaches him bowing but Garland insists on his own jazz bass approach.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: And I quit that. So I really got onto wanting to bow. I went to -- I don't know if I can recall this man's name. He used to play a trombone and he played bass, with Paul Whiteman. His name was --
No. He was President of 47, too.
And he used to make the wildest trombone. He was a double bass man. So I'd taken lessons from him on bowing.
So I started to take lessons from him, so he says to me once, he said, 'Listen, Ed, do you intend to just play strictly Dixie?' At that time, he'd say jazz.

You know? I said, 'Yeah.' He said, 'Well, I've got a selection of concert music.' (Unintelligible) I said, 'I ain't particular about that.' He said, 'Well, I'll tell you, (Unintelligible). You don't need to try to lowering the reed.' He said, 'I've taken notice. I gave you, in the lesson, just a minute ago, something to do, and I walked out of the room, and I was doing something, and you picked up the bass and (Unintelligible).' So he said, 'What are you taking lessons for?' He said, 'You don't want to learn how to play concert.' So I said, 'I know about -- a little about reading. I'm not much on it. I ain't an expert on it, but I know my notes.' But I says, 'I'll tell you, I likes my own basis for playing jazz music.' See?
I said, 'Let them other three men up in front. They're the men.' I said, 'I'll take care of the back. I'll make my own basis.'
He said, 'That sounds pretty good. That's up to you.' So he said, but if you ain't going on the
other side of the house, I don't see no need of your doing any more. Just go ahead and play like you want."
Sure. And you've been doing that very successfully.
